group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 52-year-old woman presented to the pre-anesthesia clinic five days prior to an elective outpatient right thyroid lobectomy with isthmusectomy for a 2.4-cm Bethesda IV nodule detected on ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration during evaluation of a slowly enlarging neck mass; the endocrine surgery team anticipates a two-hour procedure under general endotracheal anesthesia utilizing a low-collar transverse incision, minimal blood loss, and planned same-day discharge once voice quality, calcium levels, and pain control are confirmed satisfactory. She walked unassisted from the parking ramp, climbed one flight of stairs to reception without pausing, and conversed in full sentences throughout registration. At home she manages grocery shopping, meal preparation, and thirty-minute brisk evening walks with her dog, although she limits jogging because of arthralgia in both knees. She denies exertional chest tightness, jaw or arm pain, palpitations, syncope, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, or unexplained weight gain. Five years ago she developed sudden left-sided facial droop and clumsiness of the right hand while working; brain MRI demonstrated an acute lacunar infarct in the left internal capsule, and symptoms resolved completely after intravenous alteplase and a brief course of inpatient rehabilitation. She has had no subsequent transient neurologic episodes, carotid interventions, seizures, or cerebrovascular admissions. Coronary angiography has never been performed; a bicycle ergometry stress test ordered two years ago for pre-employment clearance reached eight metabolic equivalents without ischemic electrocardiographic changes or perfusion defects. Long-standing hypertension is managed with lisinopril 10 mg each morning and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, producing home readings in the 120s/70s. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed at age 34 when fasting plasma glucose exceeded 160 mg/dL; progressive hyperglycemia despite metformin and a sulfonylurea led to initiation of basal-bolus insulin eight years ago. She currently administers insulin glargine 24 units subcutaneously at bedtime and insulin lispro using a 1-unit-per-10-gram carbohydrate ratio before meals with a correction factor of one unit for every 25 mg/dL above 140 mg/dL. Capillary logs reviewed today show pre-breakfast values averaging 115 mg/dL and no readings below 70 mg/dL over the past month; hemoglobin A1c measured by her endocrinologist six weeks ago was 7.0 %. Additional history includes hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, seasonal allergic rhinitis, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis for which she takes acetaminophen as needed. She has never smoked, consumes a five-ounce glass of wine once weekly, and denies recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a father with a stroke at 76 and a mother with hypothyroidism; there is no premature coronary disease. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, unintentional weight change, dyspnea at rest, claudication, abdominal pain, hematuria, or easy bruising. After five minutes seated, vitals on the right arm recorded blood pressure 118/68 mm Hg, regular pulse 72 beats/minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing room air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, height 163 cm, weight 72 kg, and body mass index 27 kg/m². She appeared comfortable and euvolemic. Jugular venous contours were flat at 45 °, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the apical impulse was localized in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. Cardiac auscultation revealed crisp S1 and S2 without gallop, murmur, or rub. Lungs were clear to percussion and auscultation throughout, and there was no accessory muscle use. The neck displayed a mobile, non-tender 3-cm fullness just right of midline that moved with deglutition; no cervical lymphadenopathy or tracheal deviation was present. Abdomen was soft and non-distended, bowel sounds were normoactive, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. Extremities were warm with 2+ radial and dorsalis pedis pulses, and there was no edema or cyanosis. Neurologic screening showed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal fingertip-to-nose coordination, and a steady tandem gait. Airway evaluation demonstrated Mallampati class II, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6.5 cm, and full cervical extension. Laboratory studies drawn one hour before examination revealed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.31 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 57 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose in the same specimen was 122 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 21 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 68 U/L, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram performed in clinic displayed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/minute with normal intervals, axis, and no ST-T abnormalities when compared with a tracing from her primary-care visit six months earlier. Upright posterior-anterior chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. The anesthetic plan includes continuation of antihypertensive, statin, and antiplatelet regimens through the morning of surgery, administration of 80 % of the usual basal insulin dose the night before, withholding rapid-acting insulin once nil per os, frequent point-of-care glucose checks beginning pre-induction, and use of nerve monitoring to preserve the recurrent laryngeal nerves. Sequential compression devices will be placed intraoperatively, intravenous crystalloid will be limited to target euvolemia, and prophylactic calcium levels will be checked in the recovery area. After a detailed discussion covering potential risks of vocal cord injury, hypocalcemia, airway compromise, bleeding, recurrent stroke, and glycemic excursions, she verbalized understanding of medication timing and fasting instructions and expressed readiness to proceed with definitive thyroid surgery.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative factors:
1. High-risk surgery: 0. Thyroid lobectomy is not intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular surgery.
2. Ischemic heart disease: 0. No qualifying history or evidence of ischemia is reported.
3. Heart failure: 0. No history or clinical findings of heart failure.
4. Cerebrovascular disease: 1. The prior MRI-confirmed lacunar stroke counts despite complete recovery.
5. Preoperative insulin treatment: 1. She uses glargine and lispro.
6. Creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: 0. Her preoperative value is 1.31 mg/dL.
Total: 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
